newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: East Timor leader slams UN human rights body.
newsitem.headline: East Timor leader slams UN human rights body.

text.p: East Timor independence leader and Nobel laureate Jose Ramos Horta slammed the U.N. rights body on Thursday for failing to stand up to Indonesia and dictators.

As a row simmered over which microphone he will be allowed to used to address the 53-member body, the co-winner of the 1996 Nobel peace prize and campaigner for self-determination on the disputed island said the forum was becoming irrelevant.

Horta urged the Commission to adopt a "strongly-worded resolution" on rights abuses by Indonesia in East Timor, whose troops he accused of torture and arbitrary detention. He counted on support from European Union, the Unites States and Canada.

"This Commission isn't exactly one that looks after human rights," said Horta, an exiled ex-foreign minister of East Timor which Indonesia invaded in 1975 after Portugal withdrew from its former colony.

"The Human Rights Commission is increasingly discredited by actions of dictatorships," he told reporters on the sidelines of the annual six-week session at the U.N. European headquarters in Geneva, attended by some 2,000 officials and activists.
"If countries do not stand up to dictators, the human rights machinery created in the past 50 years will be in jeopardy."

Horta's supporters had campaigned for him to address the body from the main microphone at the podium, like previous Nobel Peace prize laureates, former Archbishop Desmond Tutu of South Africa and Rigoberta Menchu, a Guatemala-born Maya Indian.
But Indonesian delegates, backed by the African group, blocked this, saying he should only be allowed to speak from the microphone reserved for non-governmental organisations.

Diplomats said negotiations on the terms of Horta's speech, its length, subject and his seat have yet to be concluded at the Commission, an expensive operation which churned out 7,000 pages of official documents -- translated, reproduced and distributed -- at a cost of $9 million last year.
Horta said he would not address the Commission as scheduled on Thursday but hoped to later in its session in April.
Countries like China and Turkey often escape censure at the commission and many nations refrain from criticising others for fear of attacks.

Horta, who was awarded the 1996 Nobel Peace Prize along with the Roman Catholic bishop Carlos Filipe Ximenes Belo, repeated his call for a U.N.-supervised referendum on the island on whether to choose independence or integration into Indonesia.
Asked about his chances for success, he said: "We have been taught for centuries to be realistic. I am as realistic as Nelson Mandela was, I'm as realistic as the Baltic people were."
Horta said a resolution on East Timor should go beyond last year's chairman's statement, a lesser form of condemnation, and accused the forum of taking him for a fool.
"We prefer countries to tell us openly that they do not want to face Indonesia instead of pretending that we are naive and we have a low IQ level," he said.

The international community does not recognise the Roman Catholic-dominated territory's annexation. Talks under U.N. auspices between Portugal and Indonesia, aimed at finding an internationally-acceptable solution, have dragged on since 1983.
Residents believe 200,000 people were killed during the invasion, a subsequent famine and over two decades of strife.
In recent months, Horta said hundreds of East Timorese had been arrested and that the number of "private prisoners" inaccessible by the international community was soaring.
"There are hundreds of East Timorese detained at the headquarters of the military. Every army battalion, every unit and even platoons have their own prisoners," he said.
